books.section: Topic 4.4 America on the World Stage, A. Trade, Diplomacy, and the Expansion of American Influence

stimulus.text: This painting shows the transfer of Louisiana at New Orleans in 1803. In a public square, the American flag rises on a tall flagpole while the French tricolor is lowered beside it. Soldiers in uniform fire a salute, drums beat, and a crowd watches from the balconies of the buildings around the square.
stimulus.source_note: Thure de Thulstrup, Louisiana Purchase flag-raising ceremony at New Orleans, 1803; public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The United States wanted New Orleans most of all because the city

options.text: was the largest and most important city in all of North America
options.misconception: New Orleans was small; Philadelphia and New York were much larger.

options.text: controlled trade down the Mississippi River to the Gulf of Mexico
was the capital of Spanish Florida
options.misconception: Florida's capital was St. Augustine; New Orleans was the port of Louisiana.

options.text: held the only gold mines in the Louisiana Territory
options.misconception: There were no gold mines; the value was the river and the port.

rationales.A: New Orleans was a small port city in 1803. Its value was its position, not its size.
rationales.B: Western farmers shipped their crops down the Mississippi, and New Orleans sat at its mouth. Whoever held the city controlled that trade.
rationales.C: New Orleans belonged to Louisiana, not Florida. Florida's capital was St. Augustine, far to the east.
rationales.D: No gold mines made New Orleans valuable. The prize was the port at the mouth of the Mississippi River.
rationales.general:
1. Find the city on a map. New Orleans sits where the Mississippi River meets the Gulf of Mexico.
2. Ask who used the river. Western farmers floated their crops down the Mississippi to sell them abroad.
3. Put it together. Holding the city meant holding the outlet for the whole river valley's trade.
Background: Spain had closed the port to American trade in 1802, which pushed Jefferson to try to buy the city.
Remember: when a port sits at a river's mouth, ask whose goods must pass through it.
